title: Your service
tomorrow: one trait to work on. how does Amira pick just one?

cards: A church basement on a Saturday morning: folding tables, canned beans, a line out the door, volunteers who know each other by first name. On the wall, painted by someone long ago, is a line from the Gospel of Matthew.
A Muslim volunteer reads it and stops, because it sounds familiar. A hadith says something remarkably close. So what is it about serving people that two traditions put almost the same words to?

teach.h: I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.
teach.b: Here's the wall, in the King James words. Jesus tells of a king who says to the people at his right: "I was sick, and ye visited me." They ask when.

He answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Now the hadith, in Sahih Muslim. It's a hadith qudsi, in which the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reports God's own words.
On the Day of Resurrection, God says: son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me. The person asks: how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds?
God answers: didn't you know My servant was sick, and you didn't visit him?

teach.h: YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.
teach.b: Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. The same follows for food, and for water.
That's what's shared: two traditions saying that care for the sick and the hungry never stops at the person in front of you.
It reaches God. And one honest difference. Christians hear, in Matthew, Jesus the king saying the deed was done to him.
In the hadith, God doesn't become the sick person; He is found with him, near the one who needs care. Each reads its own words its own way, and neither needs the other to be wrong.
Your service is a regular place to go and find that.

how: Muslims serve through visiting the sick, food drives, mosque kitchens and neighborhood pantries, sometimes alongside churches and synagogues; visiting the sick is a practice the hadith praises directly.

o: a regular way you show up to help others
a one-time good deed during a holiday
a paid job at a mosque or religious charity

games.q: two texts, side by side — tap the pairs.
p: I was sick, and ye visited me
you would have found Me with him

s: the hadith says God becomes the sick person
it says: had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.
Matthew 25 and a hadith in Sahih Muslim both tie visiting the sick to God
'I was sick, and ye visited me'; 'I was sick and you did not visit Me.'

games.q: your floor plans a service day. one friend wants to volunteer only where people share her faith. she asks what you think. what fits today?
o: serve where you're needed. the hadith says God is found with the sick.
stick with your own community. service starts at home.
skip the day. prayer is the real service anyway.
games.why: the hadith's sick person is simply 'My servant', and the pantry on the wall says nearly the same. care for the one in front of you reaches God.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person who is sick, hungry, or alone this week: someone you know, or a face from a line somewhere. Stay with them for the sit.
Before you open your eyes, choose one regular way you could show up: a day, a place, a person.

wordCard.voice: Your service: a regular way you show up for others. In the hadith, God is found with the sick.

carryVoice: Here's your line: my service, a regular place where God is found with someone. Eight of ten, served.
